title: Pope Leo needs no further lung cancer treatment, doctors say
h1: Pope Leo XIV needs no further treatment after surgery for an early lung cancer, his doctors say
description: Pope Leo XIV's doctors said on October 21, 2026 that tests after lung surgery show the cancer had not spread and no further treatment is needed.
standfirst: Final tests confirmed a localized adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, and found no spread. His doctors say nothing medical stands in the way of a South America trip next month.
keywords: Pope Leo lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV surgery, Pope adenocarcinoma, Pope Leo South America trip
takeaways: The Pope's physician and his surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital said on October 21 that no further treatment is necessary.
Part of his right lung was removed after a nodule was found during routine exams; he left hospital on October 17.
A trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17 is expected to go ahead.
body: Pope Leo XIV will not need chemotherapy or other treatment after surgery to remove an early lung cancer, his doctors said on October 21. In a statement, his personal physician, Dr. Luigi Carbone, and his surgeon, Dr. Stefano Margaritora, chief of thoracic surgery at Rome's Gemelli hospital, said final tests confirmed an adenocarcinoma that had not spread. "A subsequent oncology assessment confirmed that no further treatment is necessary," the statement said, as reported by the Associated Press.

The nodule was an incidental finding during routine abdominal exams, and the Pope disclosed it himself at his Sunday blessing on October 11. Surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung in an operation of about 90 minutes, CBS News reported. He was discharged on Saturday, October 17, four days after surgery and earlier than the week-long stay the Vatican had anticipated.

Leo, 71, has kept working through it. He handled business from the hospital, including a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, and has since appeared at the Sunday blessing and Wednesday's general audience. It is the first significant health event of his 17-month papacy.

The Vatican has scheduled a trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, with about a dozen flights and stops at high altitude. Margaritora said there is no clinical reason to prevent it. Adenocarcinoma found early and removed surgically generally has a better outlook than lung cancer found after it spreads, which is why the incidental discovery matters. People with questions about their own lung health should talk to a physician.

faq.q: What kind of cancer did Pope Leo have?
faq.a: A localized adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, found in the lower lobe of his right lung. Tests showed it had not spread.

faq.q: Will the Pope still travel to South America?
faq.a: His surgeon said there is no clinical reason to prevent the November 6 to 17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.
